Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Tax Inspector
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Car Similarity: Similar cars
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

Vignette:
Mohammad, a 30-year-old Middle Eastern male and a tax inspector, has been experiencing significant distress following a life-threatening motor vehicle collision that occurred six months ago. The event was profoundly traumatic for him, involving a head-on crash with another vehicle while he was driving home from work. At the time of the accident, alcohol fumes were pervasive in the air due to the other driver’s intoxication, and Mohammad vividly remembers the sight of his car being hit by the oncoming vehicle. Since then, every car that looks similar to the one involved in the crash triggers intense flashbacks for Mohammad. He can hardly bear the smell of alcohol now, as it immediately transports him back to that terrifying moment. Even seeing cars on the road that resemble the one he was driving sends a wave of panic through his body. To cope with these overwhelming experiences, Mohammad has adopted several maladaptive strategies. He spends long hours engrossed in his phone or playing video games, finding solace in virtual worlds where he can momentarily escape from the reality of his trauma. Additionally, he has significantly reduced his food intake as a way to numb his emotional pain and avoid the physical discomfort that comes with it. Mohammad's hypervigilance is particularly pronounced at work. As a tax inspector, he often finds himself on high alert while conducting audits or even when sitting in meetings. The sound of an unexpected knock on the door or a sudden noise can cause him to jump out of his seat and look around warily. His colleagues have noticed this heightened state of anxiety but are unsure how to support him. The accident has deeply affected Mohammad’s self-perception, leading him to believe he cannot rely on himself anymore. He often questions whether he is still capable of performing the tasks that once defined him as a competent tax inspector. This loss of confidence extends beyond his professional life; he fears he may never feel normal emotions again and wonders if he will be able to reconnect with his former sense of self. Avoiding driving has become an almost automatic response for Mohammad, but this behavior has had significant consequences. He now frequently travels by public transportation or asks friends for rides, which has strained his relationships. His colleagues have grown concerned about his frequent absences and the impact on their team's productivity. What finally brought Mohammad to seek help was a recent incident where he experienced severe anxiety during an important audit meeting. The unexpected sound of a chair scraping against the floor caused him to panic, and he felt embarrassed by his reaction in front of his peers. This event made it clear that his symptoms were not just affecting his personal life but also his professional one. Mohammad is most afraid of losing his sense of identity and capability entirely. He hopes that therapy can help him regain a sense of control over his life and emotions, allowing him to return to the level of competence he once felt as a tax inspector. He is eager to find ways to manage his triggers without resorting to avoidance or maladaptive coping mechanisms, ultimately aiming for a more balanced and fulfilling life.
